records.rationale: Retain the generic Rust DMA-buf API used by the configured ANDROID_WRAPFD=y driver: get/put references, FD ownership transfer with error rollback, vmap ownership, bounded CPU access and paired begin/end calls. Local wrapfd/content.rs and io_context.rs use these paths and GrapheneOS libwrapfd opens /dev/wrapfd. b186055db111 adapts attachment ownership to retain ARef<Device> through map/unmap/detach, because native dma_buf_dynamic_attach stores a borrowed device pointer without get_device; the original wrapper returned an attachment independent of the borrowed device lifetime. The buffer reference was already retained. Raw addresses still require unsafe use, and device refcounting does not keep a driver bound or certify DMA resource lifetime across unbind. This change does not replace native LTS DMA implementation or add a physical-platform driver.
records.subject: ANDROID: rust: dma-buf: add base DmaBuf api

records.rationale: Retain fallible CPU-access closure variants: configured wrapfd DmaBufContent::load uses begin_cpu_access_bidirectional_fallible around io_context.read/complete. The final implementation pairs end_cpu_access after every normally returning closure, including Err; begin failure skips the closure and end, and end failure takes precedence over a closure result. Bounds and read/write const-generic access remain, with offset overflow checked before memcpy. Kernel panic is fatal, so no panic-unwind cleanup guarantee is claimed. No live CPU/device cache-coherency or file-loading test has been run.
records.subject: ANDROID: rust: dma-buf: Adds fallible begin_cpu_access*

records.rationale: Retain exporter_name and with_name for configured wrapfd fdinfo. The native dma_buf.exp_name contract explicitly says non-NULL and immutable; the Rust returned borrow is tied to the held buffer. Mutable name access is under the native name_lock and exposed only inside the closure, so an owned Rust borrow cannot escape the guard. Local wrap.rs uses the callback to format fdinfo. The callback runs under a spinlock and must not sleep; the API does not add a userspace name access bypass or change native replacement/free rules.
records.subject: ANDROID: rust: dma-buf: Adds with_name() and export_name() accessors

records.rationale: Retain the dma-buf.h bindgen include and C thunks for get_dma_buf and iosys_map memcpy to/from, together with the helpers.c inclusion. These are compilation dependencies of the selected Rust DMA-buf module and configured wrapfd driver. Native inline C implementations supply file reference increments and RAM/I/O mapping copies; the Rust CPU-access methods perform overflow/end bounds checks before invoking them. This adds no kernel userspace entry point or historical layout preservation.
records.subject: ANDROID: rust: generate bindings for dma-buf.h

records.rationale: Retain public Device::as_raw visibility as a generic vendor Rust source API. The function body remains the native Opaque raw-pointer accessor; dereferencing or passing the pointer to unsafe FFI still requires an unsafe operation and caller lifetime obligations. The local DMA-buf wrapper uses the accessor inside the kernel crate, which alone does not require public visibility. No SDK external-module consumer of the visibility widening is established; retention is conservative under the explicit vendor source customization priority, not a claim of runtime necessity or a reason to add a future reset-controller driver.
records.subject: ANDROID: rust: device: make Device::as_raw() public

records.rationale: Retain file::Offset as an exact alias of native bindings::loff_t. Configured wrapfd uses it for file/buffer ranges and checks conversions before I/O. This source typing compatibility adds no new representation, offset range or binary KMI contract; native signed offset semantics remain.
records.subject: UPSTREAM: rust: fs: add file::Offset type alias

records.rationale: Retain bindgen constants for native FMODE_READ/WRITE/CAN_READ/CAN_ODIRECT, Rust mode constants and File::mode accessor. Configured wrapfd checks FMODE_WRITE before creating/upgrading a writable wrapper and checks file capabilities in its I/O path. This exposes existing file mode bits to the source implementation; it does not authorize writes to a read-only source. The File reference pins the native file, and these wrappers do not change native access bits or LTS I/O permissions.
records.subject: ANDROID: rust: file: Adds mode constants and mode() accessor.

records.rationale: Retain the C i_size_read thunk, shared with the identical 1910f7c1f78e patch. Configured Rust ashmem uses it for ASHMEM_GET_SIZE on memfds and wrapfd checks source extents through the same native helper. It delegates to LTS i_size_read rather than introducing a raw non-atomic size read; no historical inode layout is retained. The two original patch bodies are byte-identical and represented once in the selected source.
records.subject: ANDROID: rust: file: Add a helper for reading file size from an inode

records.rationale: Retain the same i_size_read thunk as ff69fd216cba; their original patch bodies are byte-identical. Configured Rust ashmem memfd size compatibility and wrapfd extent validation call this native LTS helper. One implementation satisfies both candidates without duplicate functions or a raw inode-size load; no ABI layout preservation is added.
records.subject: ANDROID: rust: file: Add a helper for reading file size from an inode

review_method: Read the complete selected DMA-buf Rust implementation, all follow-up changes, helper files and small API patches. The base candidate introduces new files; final ACK identity before the device-reference adaptation and follow-up deltas witness its retained implementation. Read native C attach/map/unmap/detach and exporter/name contracts, local Rust Device refcounting and the selected wrapfd call sites. This does not finalize the separate whole wrapfd implementation.
local_userspace_consumer: grapheneos-17/system/memory/libwrapfd/rust/lib.rs: WrapfdDriver::new opens /dev/wrapfd; wrap uses the supplied FD and protection flags. Library presence does not prove deployment/runtime use.
